div.head: Qin slips in the Yuelu Academy collection
div.p: In the time of the Grand Supreme Emperor the Clerk of the Capital said: The sikou, the yinguan and those serving their geng turn at the Western Workshop are many of them poor and cannot provide their own grain. Deliberation: Let the Counties send the sikou to deliver grain; where a County has no grain to be lent, let it report to the County of the work-site for repayment and loan. The Western Workshop fells timber in the hills of Ju and Nanzheng; let Ju and Nanzheng act on the Western Workshop's requisitions. Those who deliver the grain, and the officers, are passed on to the Western Workshop. · In the second year it was said: Put back in use.

div.head: Appendix: text of the Zhanguo zonghengjia shu
div.p: Appendix: Your humble servant Tu went west to put questions to the King of Qin:

Your humble servant Tu went west and put questions to the King of Qin, saying: "Your servant Tu, pressing from without, wishes to have a moment of Your Majesty's standing leisure, to pour out all that his belly holds of what he has heard. At the present □ time, Yan…… Wei and the five states are joined together and advance as one. Is this for righteousness? Tu cannot know. Is it not for righteousness? Tu again cannot know, and does not know with what my King will meet it." The King did not answer. Tu again declared: "If the five states come with righteousness to make their offer, and my King meets them with righteousness, is that not righteousness? I wish my King had the means to meet them with righteousness. Those who act for righteousness all wish others to act towards them with righteousness." The King again did not answer. Tu again said: "I wish to speak further, but fear the knife and saw will not spare my body." The King said: "Speak, sir; I listen with care." Tu said: "Now Jie and Zhou were honoured as Sons of Heaven and rich in all under heaven, and lost it all. For no other reason: in every case they took unrighteousness for righteousness. The men of Wei fought the men of Yue in the wilds of Suxu, and perched the King of Yue on the summit of Kuaiji; at that time the men of Wu laid down their arms, established righteousness and served the spirits, and forced their way to be Son of Heaven; when the men of Wu did not lay down their arms, establish righteousness and serve the spirits, they lost it all, the tombs and temples of their former kings and whatever joined the great capital. For no other reason: in every case they took unrighteousness for righteousness. Now as Tu came in, the people within Your Majesty's four borders all had the look of hunger and cold; I privately asked the reason, and they said: 'How we hate the use of arms!' The soldiers of Yinjin and Shangluo are the finest soldiers under heaven; since Fengqi they have taken heads six times. Now going out to battle they cannot win, and keeping guard within they cannot hold firm; they cannot hold their walls, and the five punishments pass over their bodies, yet they cannot feel it as shame. For no other reason: in every case they have never been stood down. Ganjiang and Moye are the finest swords under heaven; tried on metal □ … □□□□□□ … never let go …; Lü'er is the finest horse under heaven; driven on the road under heavy loads for long and never let go, a worn-out nag □ arrives. For no other reason: in every case they have never been stood down. To attack armies and kill generals is the King's gain, but it is the people's strength. The people put their bodies to the cord to have their heads cut off and their bellies ripped; … taken □□ bodies, moved away to garrison in anxious guard, this too is a great calamity. That by which a king of ten thousand chariots □ [on] □ □: some desire gold, pearls and jade, racing horses, □ hunting and listening to music, and so, hearing the persuaders tell of the ease of attack and the profit of gaining land, the great among them pledge several hundred [chariots] and the □ several tens, and carry silks and gifts to □ the Lords; and surely next morning they raise an army □ to □ the border. The men who stay in the army do not □□□□□□□ … the ranks: the longest for several years, the □ for a full year. The levy raised and the land brought under rule, a territory not □ a hundred-odd li around, and land that cannot be left empty, so that the people of the interior □ must be moved to fill it; the common people are not at ease and moreover □: can this be? Why does the King not halt the troops and raise none, and order them to stay at home, grant them their plans (?) □, repair their walls, and further □ one another, so that at home they have their joy and the arrears of levies are all rewarded? In Tu's private view, this is the finest policy under heaven. The Yellow Emperor □ said: at three hundred years of age □, straighten the body, □ examine, and then know sufficiency. Now my King's land bags (?) Chu to the south-east and halves Zhao to the north, all of it [fertile] land. To the west it reaches where the sun goes in, to the □ of no armour; that its soldiers are strong and its people many, none does not know. It has besides forests of zui'ao, bifang, cherry and plum, orange and pomelo, loquat and purple ginger; islets of zhonglong and xujian; caves of fine cinnabar; and shoals of ganle, □□, palm and peach-branch; of the myriad things there is none it lacks."
